summary:
Mars Survival Guide is a bilingual, interactive educational platform created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to explore a central question: how can humans prepare to survive, work, and thrive on Mars? It brings together three connected dimensions of a future mission: planetary exploration, sustainable food production, and human well-being.

Mars Maps turns NASA imagery and planetary data into an interactive exploration of Jezero Crater. Users can examine scientific layers, mark locations, plan hypothetical routes—including experimental terrain-aware paths—and organize mission records. Mars Greenhouse features an inventory of 18 crop and biofactory categories, 3D plant visualizations, and interactive controls for water, light, and temperature to illustrate cultivation challenges and plant stress. Mind Space addresses the human side of exploration with a private mission journal, self-reported indicators such as sleep, mood, and stress, and reflective activities focused on life far from Earth.

By connecting scientific evidence with hands-on exploration, the platform makes complex research approachable for students and curious audiences. It emphasizes that a successful Mars mission requires not only engineering, but also responsible resource use, food-system resilience, and attention to astronauts’ psychological and physical needs. The simulations are educational tools, not operational mission predictions.
details:
Project Details — Mars Survival Guide

Team: Lagrange Points - Brazil

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

1. Project Overview: Preparing Humanity for Life on Mars

Mars Survival Guide is an interactive, bilingual web platform developed by Lagrange Points - Brazil for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project addresses the challenge of understanding and preparing for human survival on Mars by combining planetary exploration, sustainable food production, and astronaut health into a unified educational environment.

Rather than approaching Martian survival exclusively as a technological challenge, we recognize it as an interconnected scientific and human problem. Establishing a sustainable presence on another planet requires understanding the terrain, identifying environmental constraints, developing reliable life-support systems, producing food in controlled habitats, and maintaining the physical and psychological well-being of crews living far from Earth.

Our platform translates scientific research and publicly available planetary data into accessible interactive experiences. It allows users to explore Martian geography, investigate potential exploration routes, study hypothetical crop responses to environmental conditions, and reflect on the human challenges of long-duration space missions.

The project is organized into three complementary modules:

  • Mars Maps: Planetary exploration, geographic visualization, route planning, and scientific mission analysis.
  • Mars Greenhouse: Space agriculture, controlled-environment cultivation, biological resources, and interactive crop simulations.
  • Mind Space: Astronaut psychological and physical well-being, personal monitoring, reflection, and adaptation to isolated environments.

These modules form a multidisciplinary educational guide centered on a fundamental principle: surviving on Mars requires understanding both the planet and the people who will explore it.

The platform is publicly accessible at https://www.marsurvivalguide.club and offers interfaces in Portuguese and English.

2. Mars Maps — Scientific Exploration and Mission Planning

Mars Maps is the central geographic component of Mars Survival Guide and the foundation of our response to the challenge.

Its main objective is to transform real planetary data into an interactive environment where users can understand Martian terrain, explore scientifically relevant locations, and investigate the challenges of planning missions on another planet.

2.1. Real NASA Data and Planetary Visualization

Mars Maps incorporates planetary imagery and geospatial information from NASA and the United States Geological Survey (USGS).

The application uses NASA's Mars Trek infrastructure, particularly Web Map Tile Service (WMTS) resources, to display scientific cartographic information. Its active orbital base map includes the Mars Global Surveyor's Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) global shaded-relief product, providing a scientific representation of Martian topography.

Users can navigate the map through zooming, panning, and interactive controls.

The platform also includes an officially sourced image of Jezero Crater from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter mission, credited to NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona. This image serves as an alternative visualization when the online planetary service is unavailable.

Importantly, the image-based visualization is explicitly identified as schematic when geographic coordinates cannot be reliably projected onto it.

Our development process also investigated higher-resolution CTX and HiRISE orbital products, including mosaics associated with the Mars 2020 mission. These sources informed the project's scientific and cartographic research, while the current map interface distinguishes between the planetary layers actually available to users and other products examined during development.

2.2. Exploration of Jezero Crater

Jezero Crater was selected as the platform's principal exploration region because of its scientific relevance to NASA's Mars 2020 Perseverance mission.

The region contains geological formations associated with the planet's history of water, including an ancient delta system that makes it particularly interesting for understanding past environmental conditions and investigating potential biosignatures.

The application highlights three scientifically relevant locations:

Belva Crater: A crater in the Jezero delta region whose exposed geological layers provide opportunities to investigate sedimentary structures and local geological history.

Neretva Vallis: A valley associated with the geological and hydrological evolution of the Jezero region.

Jezero Crater: The broader scientific region selected for the Mars 2020 mission, associated with the investigation of ancient environments and the history of water on Mars.

Each location includes contextual scientific information, geographic coordinates, mission associations, and links to supporting sources.

The coordinates are based on the USGS/International Astronomical Union planetary nomenclature catalog, using Martian coordinate conventions rather than treating the planet as Earth.

These catalog coordinates represent approximate feature centers, not surveyed astronaut destinations or exact sample collection points.

2.3. Interactive Route Planning

A central feature is Marswalk, an interactive tool for designing hypothetical exploration routes across the Martian surface.

Users can select an origin and destination, visualize a connection between locations, and estimate the geographical distance between them.

The mathematical calculations use a spherical approximation of Mars, with a radius of 3,396,190 meters, rather than Earth's radius.

The application computes great-circle distances using spherical geometry, allowing the estimated distances to reflect Martian planetary dimensions.

Users can:

  • Select scientific locations as starting points or destinations.
  • Create their own geographic markers.
  • Enter coordinates manually.
  • Name and describe personalized locations.
  • Classify markers according to their purpose.
  • Identify locations as visited or not visited in their records.
  • Edit or remove markers.
  • Reverse or clear a proposed route.
  • Save and reopen mission plans.

Custom markers can represent exploration objectives, resources, scientific interests, hazards, or other user-defined locations.

2.4. Terrain-Aware Route Exploration

Beyond geometric distance calculations, the platform implements an experimental terrain-aware routing system.

This functionality uses a real digital elevation model (DEM) derived from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Context Camera (CTX) imagery and distributed through USGS Astrogeology resources.

The original elevation product has a nominal projected resolution of 20 meters. For the application, a defined portion of the Jezero region was processed into a 100-meter computational grid.

The route-planning algorithm uses A-star (A) pathfinding*, a graph-search technique that evaluates possible connections between locations.

The experimental cost function incorporates horizontal distance, estimated elevation differences, and terrain slope penalties.

Users can compare a direct geometric route with a terrain-aware alternative and examine available metrics such as:

  • Estimated route distance.
  • Differences between direct and terrain-aware routes.
  • Approximate cumulative ascent and descent.
  • Maximum estimated terrain inclination.
  • The effects of different slope constraints.

Users can select experimental maximum-slope parameters to investigate how terrain restrictions influence the available routes.

These calculations are performed within the coverage and resolution of the available elevation model.

The algorithm does not simulate every obstacle, soil stability, astronaut movement, rover capabilities, energy consumption, or environmental hazard. Accordingly, the results are explicitly presented as educational estimates rather than certified safe routes or operational navigation plans.

This distinction is particularly important when using real scientific datasets in a public-facing educational application.

2.5. Mission Organization and Exploration Library

Mars Maps provides a structured workflow with three stages:

Planning: Users select locations, establish route parameters, and prepare an exploration.

Exploration: Users review the planned path, geographic context, and available mission measurements.

Analysis: Users examine the route summary, associated markers, mission information, and available metrics before finalizing their exploration record.

The application also includes a mission management interface, allowing users to create and maintain plans with identifying information, objectives, dates, and descriptions.

Completed analyses can be saved in a dedicated Exploration Library.

Within this library, users can search, filter, organize, review, rename, delete, and reopen saved explorations.

This encourages repeated investigation and comparison of different exploration plans rather than treating the map as a passive image viewer.

An interactive guided tutorial introduces the main tools, improving usability for first-time visitors.

2.6. Why Mars Maps Matters

Planetary exploration is essential to understanding where and how humans could eventually operate on Mars.

Terrain, geographic distances, geological context, and access to scientific resources influence mission planning and the development of future infrastructure.

Our platform allows users to interact with these considerations through real planetary datasets and transparent mathematical methods.

It also encourages scientific reasoning by making the differences between geographic distance, terrain-derived route estimates, and real operational safety explicit.

3. Mars Greenhouse — Food Production and Biological Life Support

Mars Greenhouse explores one of the greatest challenges associated with prolonged human missions: maintaining a sustainable and reliable food supply far from Earth.

Transporting all necessary food and biological resources from Earth would create logistical constraints for long-duration missions.

Studying controlled-environment agriculture, food diversity, biological systems, and resource recycling is therefore important for future exploration.

Our module presents these subjects through an interactive crop inventory and a visual environmental simulation.

3.1. Interactive Agricultural Inventory

Mars Greenhouse features 18 agricultural and biological production categories, compiled from the team's technical research and contextualized with scientific literature.

The inventory includes:

  1. Potatoes.
  2. Sweet potatoes.
  3. Dwarf wheat.
  4. Rye.
  5. Dwarf rice.
  6. Quinoa.
  7. Soybeans.
  8. Peanuts.
  9. Cowpeas and peas.
  10. Dwarf tomatoes.
  11. Dwarf peppers.
  12. Lettuce and other leafy vegetables.
  13. Brassicas.
  14. Garden cress and mustard.
  15. Radishes, carrots, and beets.
  16. Cucumbers and dwarf strawberries.
  17. Sweet clover and Lotus species.
  18. Edible microbial biomass and a conceptual biological production system.

These categories represent different potential contributions to a food-production strategy, including carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, micronutrients, dietary diversity, and biological resource management.

Users can search the inventory, filter agricultural categories, and select individual entries for detailed examination.

Each category presents relevant information such as common and scientific names, species or cultivars, nutritional contributions, potential cultivation methods, proposed cultivation cycles, environmental references, limitations, and scientific sources.

The catalog distinguishes established research from engineering assumptions and educational approximations.

The inclusion of microbial biomass broadens the discussion beyond conventional agriculture, introducing biological production systems as a possible subject of future space-life-support research.

3.2. Interactive 3D Plant Visualization

One of the module's main creative features is the integration of interactive three-dimensional visualizations.

Using procedural graphics developed with Three.js, the platform represents different crop groups through models reflecting broad morphological characteristics.

These models distinguish elements such as leaves, roots, stems, fruits, tubers, cereals, and biological production structures.

Users can rotate and zoom the visualizations to inspect them from different perspectives.

The application also includes a visual representation of a conceptual photobioreactor for the microbial production category.

The models are designed for educational interaction and are not anatomically precise reconstructions of specific cultivars.

When advanced WebGL visualization is unavailable, the interface provides a compatible fallback representation.

3.3. Environmental Control Simulation

The central interactive feature allows users to modify three environmental variables:

Water availability: Representing moisture-related conditions and the potential consequences of water deficit or excess.

Light intensity: Exploring how insufficient or excessive illumination could influence plant appearance.

Temperature: Demonstrating conceptual responses to conditions below or above the selected reference ranges.

The application compares user-selected values with documented reference intervals for the selected category.

These intervals are identified according to their origin, such as proposed engineering targets, values derived from the team's dossier, or educational approximations.

For example, the team's reference material includes a general treated-substrate moisture range of 25–35% and a proposed LED photosynthetic photon flux density range of 200–300 micromoles per square meter per second. These are presented with appropriate qualifications rather than treated as universal biological optima.

When the user changes an environmental variable, the 3D representation responds visually.

Low water availability may produce drooping or changes in coloration. Excess moisture may alter the appearance of the root environment. Reduced light may produce illustrative elongation or paler leaves. Temperature deviations generate other visual changes.

The simulation also provides written explanations identifying the main factor outside the selected reference range, possible visible symptoms, and adjustments that could return the scenario to its reference conditions.

3.4. Environmental Stress, Accumulated Damage, and Recovery

Rather than instantly damaging a plant whenever a slider is moved, our system distinguishes between current environmental stress and illustrative accumulated damage.

Environmental stress is assessed immediately through a transparent heuristic scoring system.

Accumulated damage, however, progresses only when the user manually advances an exposure stage.

The interface includes controls to:

  • Advance a stage of environmental exposure.
  • Observe accumulated visual damage.
  • Restore the environmental reference settings.
  • Advance a recovery stage when conditions are appropriate.
  • Reset the illustrative damage state.

This structure allows users to explore how repeated exposure to unsuitable conditions differs conceptually from a temporary environmental deviation.

The manual stages do not represent actual biological time, and the simulation does not predict crop mortality, biomass production, growth rates, or real physiological responses.

Its purpose is to make environmental relationships easier to understand and investigate.

3.5. Scientific Foundation of Mars Greenhouse

The module draws on research into controlled-environment agriculture and plant cultivation in space.

Important scientific references include NASA's Veggie experiments, the Advanced Plant Habitat, the XROOTS investigation of hydroponic and aeroponic systems, and research on specific crops aboard the International Space Station.

The project also considers the NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document as a contextual engineering reference.

Research by Wamelink and collaborators on plant growth in simulated Martian and lunar soils contributes to the discussion of potential cultivation substrates.

Studies of UV-resistant terrestrial microorganisms, including research involving organisms from the Atacama Desert, provide additional context for the investigation of biological resilience and future microbial applications.

USDA FoodData Central serves as a reference for studying the nutritional composition of terrestrial foods.

Our team considered several environmental requirements for future Martian agriculture:

Atmospheric protection: Plants cannot be assumed to grow directly on the unprotected Martian surface. Cultivation requires a suitable controlled environment.

Radiation protection: A greenhouse would require protection against radiation exposure.

Water management: Water is a limited and valuable resource whose treatment, reuse, and controlled delivery would be essential.

Nutrient management: Crop production requires appropriate nutrient availability and monitoring.

Artificial illumination: Lighting intensity, spectrum, and photoperiod would need to be adapted to cultivation requirements.

Temperature regulation: Environmental control is fundamental to crop development and system reliability.

Substrate safety: Untreated Martian regolith must not be considered immediately suitable agricultural soil. Potential contaminants, including perchlorates, require careful assessment and remediation research.

Crop diversity: Nutritional balance, resource demands, crop cycles, and redundancy are relevant considerations for a future food system.

The team's broader mission research considered Arcadia Planitia as a hypothetical scenario for future resource and habitat planning. However, the greenhouse application does not claim to model an operational facility at that location, and its geographic scenario is kept distinct from the Jezero exploration map.

3.6. Why Mars Greenhouse Matters

Mars Greenhouse makes the challenges of space agriculture understandable through direct experimentation.

Instead of simply reading that plants need appropriate environmental conditions, users can investigate how changes in water, light, and temperature influence the illustrative state of different agricultural categories.

The module also demonstrates why sustainable food production involves more than selecting a single crop. Nutritional diversity, cultivation technology, environmental control, resource availability, and biological limitations must be considered together.

The result is an educational tool that connects biology, chemistry, agriculture, and space-life-support engineering.

4. Mind Space — Psychological and Physical Well-Being

Mind Space focuses on an aspect of interplanetary exploration that is sometimes overshadowed by rockets, habitats, and planetary engineering: the humans participating in the mission.

A journey to Mars would involve prolonged isolation, confinement, delayed communication with Earth, demanding routines, environmental restrictions, and limited access to familiar support systems.

These conditions make human factors an essential component of mission preparation.

Mind Space was developed to encourage reflection on psychological and physical well-being through an interactive personal mission journal and educational activities.

4.1. Personal Mission Journal

The platform includes a daily journal designed around five self-reported indicators:

Emotional state: How the user perceives their emotional condition.

Energy level: Their subjective experience of physical and mental energy.

Sleep quality: Their personal evaluation of rest and sleep.

Perceived stress: Their own assessment of stress.

Perceived physical condition: How they evaluate their physical state on that day.

Each dimension uses a five-point scale, with contextual descriptions that support personal reflection.

Users can also record the mission date and add optional written observations.

The journal applies a one-submission-per-local-calendar-day policy. Editing an entry is also treated as a submission under this policy.

Saved records can be reviewed through the history interface, with editing and deletion options subject to the application's daily-entry rules.

4.2. Personal Trends and Visualization

Mind Space goes beyond an individual check-in by presenting previously recorded information through an interactive dashboard.

The dashboard includes:

  • The number of registered days.
  • Summary averages for selected indicators.
  • Visual charts covering recent entries.
  • Comparisons between recent and earlier records when enough information is available.
  • A chronological history of personal records.
  • Detailed views of individual entries.
  • Educational suggestions for reflection.

These features encourage users to observe their experiences over time rather than focusing exclusively on a single day.

For instance, someone exploring a hypothetical long-duration mission can reflect on how changing routines, stress, and sleep might relate to their perceived well-being.

The data remain subjective personal reports. The application does not infer medical diagnoses or calculate validated clinical risk scores.

4.3. Meditation Timer and Personal Reflection

Mind Space includes a simple meditation timer that allows users to track the duration of a personal pause.

It supports starting, pausing, resuming, and resetting the timer.

This feature is intended as an optional reflective activity that users may incorporate into their routine.

The tool does not impose a breathing protocol, provide psychological treatment, or claim that the practice has a specific medical effect.

4.4. Interactive Human-Factors Scenarios

The application also presents three educational scenarios inspired by challenges studied in human spaceflight research.

Isolation — A Week Away from Home

This scenario explores the emotional and social challenges of living far from familiar environments.

It encourages reflection on meaningful routines, maintaining relationships, and recognizing personal needs.

Communication — When Earth's Answer Does Not Arrive Immediately

This scenario addresses the communication delays associated with distant space missions.

Users explore the importance of organizing information, communicating clearly, managing expectations, and relying on local crew support when immediate responses from Earth are unavailable.

Teamwork and Stress — Living Together Under Pressure

This scenario explores interpersonal challenges in a confined and demanding environment.

It presents educational strategies involving respectful communication, recognizing fatigue, listening to other perspectives, and maintaining shared objectives.

These interactive situations are fictional educational exercises, not validated astronaut-training protocols.

4.5. Scientific Foundation and Privacy

Mind Space was informed by NASA research concerning isolation, confinement, behavioral health, sleep, fatigue, and human adaptation to spaceflight.

Our broader research also considered NASA Human Research Program evidence reports, human-system standards, and studies involving physiological and behavioral monitoring.

Research into wearable technologies and spaceflight health monitoring, including the Canadian Space Agency's Bio-Monitor, helped contextualize possibilities for future development.

However, the current platform does not connect to physical wearables, automatically collect physiological telemetry, or perform clinical evaluation.

Privacy was a major consideration.

Personal journal information is stored locally in the user's browser rather than transmitted to a centralized application database.

No account is required to use the journal.

This approach allows users to explore personal monitoring without creating a remote repository of sensitive wellness entries.

The limitation is that records are associated with the browser and device where they were created; they are not automatically synchronized between devices.

4.6. Why Mind Space Matters

Human survival cannot be understood exclusively through environmental engineering.

A scientifically successful expedition must also consider how people cope with long periods away from Earth, demanding work, limited privacy, communication difficulties, and changes in daily routine.

Mind Space introduces these subjects through accessible tools that encourage awareness, reflection, and informed discussion.

By placing human well-being alongside exploration and agriculture, our platform emphasizes that astronauts are not simply operators of technological systems: they are individuals whose needs form part of mission sustainability.

5. Integration: One Mission, Three Perspectives

The primary innovation of Mars Survival Guide is the integration of three disciplines that are often presented separately.

Mars Maps examines the physical environment and the challenges of operating on Martian terrain.

Mars Greenhouse investigates potential approaches to producing food and supporting biological systems inside protected habitats.

Mind Space explores the human experience of participating in a prolonged mission.

Together, these modules create a broader understanding of what sustaining a human presence on Mars could involve.

For example, a user can begin by investigating a scientifically relevant region of Mars, creating a hypothetical exploration route, and studying its geographic characteristics.

The same user can then explore the environmental demands of food production by modifying greenhouse conditions and observing illustrative biological responses.

Finally, the user can reflect on the effects of isolation, stress, communication delays, and personal routines through Mind Space.

This progression connects planetary conditions, resource management, biological systems, and crew well-being within a shared educational narrative.

The modules do not claim to constitute a fully integrated operational mission simulator. Rather, they provide complementary learning experiences that encourage multidisciplinary reasoning.

This approach reflects the complexity of real interplanetary challenges, where success depends on understanding relationships between many scientific and engineering systems.

6. Technologies, Programming Languages, and Development Tools

Mars Survival Guide was developed as a modern web application using accessible, widely adopted technologies.

6.1. Application Architecture

The project uses:

Next.js 16: The main web application framework, providing routing, rendering infrastructure, and application organization through the App Router.

React 19: The component-based interface library responsible for interactive elements, application state, forms, and reactive visualizations.

TypeScript: The primary programming language, used with strict type checking to improve code organization, maintainability, and reliability.

JavaScript: Used for development tooling, supporting scripts, and runtime functionality.

HTML and CSS: Used to structure and style the application.

CSS Modules: Used to organize component-specific styles, alongside global design tokens.

Lucide React: Used for interface icons and visual navigation elements.

The application follows a modular architecture, separating presentation components, scientific datasets, mathematical calculations, simulation logic, and persistent browser records.

6.2. Planetary Mapping Technologies

The geographic module uses:

Leaflet: An interactive mapping library supporting zooming, panning, layers, and markers.

React Leaflet: Integration between Leaflet and React components.

NASA Mars Trek WMTS: An external source for planetary cartographic tiles and associated service metadata.

Custom Martian coordinate and projection logic: Developed to handle planetary latitude and longitude without incorrectly assuming Earth's geographic reference system.

Great-circle distance calculations: Used to approximate distances on a spherical model of Mars.

A-star pathfinding: Used for experimental terrain-aware route calculations.

Digital elevation model processing: Used to transform a scientific elevation dataset into a computational representation suitable for browser-based route exploration.

GeoTIFF processing tools: Used during preparation of the terrain dataset.

Web Workers: Used to perform computationally demanding route calculations without unnecessarily blocking the user interface.

The terrain implementation includes data-integrity checks, error handling, and caching mechanisms.

6.3. Three-Dimensional Simulation Technologies

Mars Greenhouse uses Three.js and WebGL for interactive procedural 3D graphics.

Instead of relying exclusively on static images, we developed models whose appearance responds to simulated environmental conditions.

The system connects environmental controls with visual properties such as coloration, posture, illumination, and accumulated stress effects.

Fallback visualizations improve compatibility when the main 3D rendering environment is unavailable.

6.4. Data Storage and User Interaction

The platform uses browser-local storage for features such as mission records, exploration history, user-created markers, journal entries, and language preferences.

This allows meaningful interaction without requiring an account or dedicated application database.

The architecture is primarily client-oriented, with external requests used where appropriate to retrieve planetary map resources.

No physical hardware, environmental sensor, biological cultivation device, astronaut wearable, or rover was required to build or operate the current prototype.

The project is a software-based educational platform, not a physical Mars habitat experiment.

6.5. Development, Testing, and Deployment

The development environment includes:

Node.js and npm: Application execution and dependency management.

Git and GitHub: Version control, collaboration, branch management, and source-code hosting.

ESLint: Static code quality checks.

TypeScript type checking: Verification of type consistency.

Vitest: Automated unit and interface tests.

React Testing Library: Tests focused on user-interface behavior.

JSDOM: A simulated browser environment for automated component testing.

Node.js testing tools: Additional tests for mathematical calculations and application behavior.

The source repository also contains tests for cartographic calculations, map interactions, state management, saved records, terrain routing, and scientific interface logic.

The public application is deployed through web-hosting infrastructure and made available under its own custom domain.

The project does not depend on a paid API subscription, separate authentication service, or secret API credentials for its core functions.

7. Scientific Data, APIs, and Research Sources

A major consideration during development was the responsible use of scientific information.

The team investigated planetary science, astrobiology, crop production, resource utilization, and human factors using publications and technical materials from NASA and other research institutions.

The principal sources include:

NASA Mars Trek: Planetary cartographic services and imagery distribution.

Mars Global Surveyor / MOLA: Global Martian topographic context.

Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter: Scientific imagery and terrain datasets relevant to the Jezero region.

NASA Mars 2020 / Perseverance: Geological exploration context and the scientific significance of Jezero Crater.

USGS Astrogeology Science Center: Planetary terrain products, digital elevation models, and related mapping resources.

USGS/IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature: Published feature names and approximate geographic coordinates.

NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS): Technical publications addressing space-life-support research, mission engineering, environmental challenges, and human health.

NASA Space Biology and Plant Research: Research involving controlled plant growth and biological investigations in space.

NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR): Scientific material relating to space biology, including studies associated with plant experiments, microbiomes, and transcriptomics considered during the team's research.

USDA FoodData Central: Terrestrial nutritional composition data used as scientific context for the agricultural inventory.

Peer-reviewed scientific literature: Research on Martian and lunar soil simulants, biological resilience, planetary conditions, food-production systems, and long-duration spaceflight challenges.

NASA Human Research Program: Evidence and research concerning behavioral health, sleep, fatigue, human performance, and adaptation to isolated spaceflight environments.

The broader research also examined topics such as subsurface water ice, perchlorate contamination, radiation exposure, environmental monitoring, and biomedical wearable technologies.

These subjects informed the team's understanding of potential mission constraints and future opportunities, but not all of them are implemented as live maps, monitoring systems, or simulations in the current software.

We deliberately distinguished between data directly consumed by the application, local datasets processed for the prototype, scientific references supporting educational content, and concepts proposed for future development.

This separation was essential for maintaining scientific transparency.

8. Design, Accessibility, and User Experience

One of our design objectives was to make technically complex subjects understandable to users without requiring prior expertise in planetary science or advanced programming.

The interface uses the visual language of a mission atlas, combining a dark space-inspired aesthetic with distinct visual identities for each module.

Orange represents geographic exploration and mission planning.

Green represents agriculture, biological systems, and sustainable cultivation.

Blue represents human factors, reflection, and well-being.

These visual distinctions help users recognize the role of each module while maintaining a unified identity across the application.

The website was designed for responsive use across different screen sizes, including desktop and mobile layouts.

The implementation also considers:

  • Clear navigation between modules.
  • Descriptive labels and accessible form controls.
  • Visible interactive states.
  • Keyboard-oriented interaction alternatives.
  • Guided explanations and tutorials.
  • Readable scientific descriptions.
  • Explanations of unavailable data or unsupported operations.
  • Graceful fallback behavior where external or graphical resources fail.
  • Language accessibility through Portuguese and English interfaces.

The project combines structured scientific information with interactive visual exploration, helping users learn through observation, experimentation, and reflection.

Although accessibility was considered during development, the project does not claim formal certification against a particular accessibility standard.

9. Creativity and Innovation

The originality of Mars Survival Guide does not depend on claiming to discover new Martian data or to replace professional mission-planning systems.

Instead, its innovation lies in transforming diverse scientific resources into a coherent, interactive educational experience.

Several aspects distinguish the project.

Connecting Multiple Survival Systems

Many educational experiences focus on a single aspect of space exploration.

Our platform connects geography, food production, and human well-being, encouraging users to understand Martian survival as an interconnected challenge.

Turning Real Planetary Data into Exploration Activities

Mars Maps does more than display images of Mars.

It allows users to identify scientific regions, construct routes, create custom markers, analyze available geographic measurements, and maintain an exploration library.

This transforms passive observation into an active investigation.

Combining Mathematical Models with Geographic Interaction

The platform includes calculations adapted to Martian geometry and an experimental terrain-aware pathfinding system.

Rather than simply drawing a line between two locations, users can investigate why the shortest geometric connection may differ from a terrain-constrained route.

Visualizing Biological Concepts in 3D

Mars Greenhouse turns environmental variables into visible changes in plant representations.

This makes abstract discussions of cultivation requirements more intuitive and supports interactive exploration of environmental stress.

The separation between immediate stress and accumulated damage introduces an additional educational dimension.

Including Human Well-Being as Part of Mission Sustainability

Mind Space broadens the definition of survival by emphasizing routines, personal perception, communication, and psychological adaptation.

The combination of personal reflection, historical visualization, and fictional mission scenarios creates an experience that goes beyond conventional scientific information pages.

Making Research Accessible

The application presents specialized scientific material through understandable descriptions, visual tools, and practical interactions.

Its bilingual approach also supports participation by Portuguese-speaking and English-speaking audiences.

Maintaining Scientific Transparency

A further distinguishing decision was to explain limitations directly within the user experience.

The platform identifies when information comes from verified scientific observations, published datasets, proposed engineering assumptions, or illustrative models.

This encourages responsible interpretation of scientific information rather than presenting simplified demonstrations as operational predictions.

10. Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered multiple scientific, technical, and human factors when designing the project.

Martian Environmental Conditions

Mars presents substantial challenges, including a thin atmosphere, low temperatures, radiation exposure, dust, limited accessible water, and terrain-related uncertainties.

These conditions affect mobility, human health, agriculture, and infrastructure design.

The project incorporates selected aspects of these challenges in its educational modules and discusses others as broader mission constraints.

Resource Availability and Sustainability

Potential water resources, efficient cultivation, environmental control, resource recycling, nutritional diversity, and reduced dependence on Earth are important considerations for long-term missions.

Our agricultural research emphasizes that sustainability is a system-level issue, not simply the ability to grow individual plants.

Scientific Accuracy and Data Provenance

We sought to use identifiable sources and document the origin and limitations of scientific data.

Planetary coordinate systems, elevation models, simulated environmental ranges, and biological references require careful interpretation.

For example, observations from plant experiments aboard the International Space Station cannot automatically be considered proof that the same crops would grow successfully on Mars.

Similarly, Martian terrain calculations cannot establish operational safety without additional information and validation.

Human Needs

We considered the challenges of isolation, emotional adaptation, stress, sleep, communication delays, workload, and relationships within confined teams.

This led us to include human well-being as a distinct but equally important project component.

Computational Efficiency and Reliability

Interactive planetary maps and 3D visualizations can require significant computing resources.

The project therefore incorporates techniques such as client-side dynamic component loading, dedicated terrain-calculation workers, local scientific datasets, and fallback displays.

The interface also includes error handling for unavailable map services and data outside supported geographic coverage.

Privacy and Data Management

We considered the sensitivity of personal reflections and the practical requirements of saving user-created exploration records.

Browser-based storage provides a straightforward solution for this educational prototype without requiring account creation or the transmission of personal wellness entries to a project-managed server.

Educational Value

Another important consideration was avoiding unnecessary complexity for users encountering the subjects for the first time.

We therefore prioritized explanatory feedback, intuitive controls, scientific source references, interactive experimentation, and visually distinct modules.

Multidisciplinary Collaboration

The project brought together research and development challenges spanning planetary science, chemistry, biology, agriculture, software engineering, data visualization, and human factors.

The three-module structure allowed different research fronts to contribute to a shared platform while preserving the scientific purpose of each area.

11. Benefits and Intended Impact

Mars Survival Guide was designed to create educational, scientific, and social value.

Supporting STEM Education

The platform provides an approachable introduction to planetary science, geography, mathematical modeling, biology, chemistry, agriculture, and human spaceflight.

Students can interact with scientific concepts instead of encountering them exclusively through textbooks or presentations.

Encouraging Scientific Curiosity

Exploring real Martian terrain and investigating hypothetical mission problems can encourage users to ask questions about the environment, scientific evidence, engineering limitations, and future research opportunities.

Promoting Systems Thinking

The integration of terrain, agriculture, and human health helps demonstrate how different disciplines influence one another.

It encourages users to think beyond isolated technological solutions and consider the broader requirements for sustaining human life.

Increasing Awareness of Space Agriculture

The greenhouse module introduces food production as a complex scientific challenge involving controlled environments, nutritional resources, water, energy, substrates, and biological responses.

Emphasizing Astronaut Well-Being

The project reinforces the importance of sleep, emotional awareness, teamwork, communication, and individual adaptation in long-duration exploration.

Improving Access to Public Scientific Research

By using publicly available information and widely adopted web technologies, the platform makes selected NASA and partner research resources more accessible to non-specialist audiences.

Enabling Continued Educational Use

The saved exploration features, interactive simulations, and personal journal encourage repeated engagement rather than a one-time visit.

The project can support classroom demonstrations, science outreach activities, and independent learning.

Connecting Space Exploration with Challenges on Earth

Although focused on Mars, the project encourages reflection on issues that also matter on Earth: sustainable agriculture, efficient water use, environmental monitoring, psychological well-being, scientific literacy, and responsible resource management.

Solutions developed for extreme environments can inspire new questions and approaches to terrestrial sustainability.

The platform does not claim to have developed or experimentally validated such technologies; its contribution is to support understanding and exploration of the underlying challenges.

12. Scientific Limitations and Responsible Communication

Scientific credibility is a fundamental aspect of the project.

Mars Survival Guide is an independent educational prototype and is not endorsed by NASA.

Its use of NASA and partner datasets does not make the platform an official mission-planning, biomedical, or agricultural decision-support system.

The Mars Maps module uses real geographic data, but its route calculations are approximations with explicit spatial, resolution, and environmental limitations.

The current terrain model does not account for every obstacle or factor required to establish safe movement across Mars.

The Mars Greenhouse module uses research-informed references and illustrative environmental responses, but its simulations are not validated biological growth or crop-survival models.

The 3D representations do not predict agricultural yield or establish the feasibility of operating a particular crop-production system on Mars.

Mind Space offers educational self-reflection tools, not diagnosis, treatment, medical monitoring, or validated psychological assessment.

Likewise, the use of published spaceflight studies does not imply that the project has tested its features with astronauts or conducted physical experiments in Martian conditions.

These limitations are intentional and documented.

We believe that communicating uncertainty clearly is an essential part of scientific education, particularly when transforming complex research into interactive public-facing tools.

13. Future Development Opportunities

The current platform establishes a foundation for further educational and technical development.

Potential future extensions include:

Expanded planetary coverage: Additional scientifically verified map layers and geographic regions beyond the current Jezero-centered experience.

Improved terrain analysis: Higher-resolution validated elevation products, additional environmental constraints, and more detailed exploration metrics.

Resource investigation: Educational visualization of potential subsurface ice, local resources, and environmental constraints, informed by relevant planetary science datasets.

Advanced greenhouse modeling: Further literature review and development of quantitative biological models where sufficient experimental evidence becomes available.

Life-support systems integration: Educational representations of interactions among water recycling, food production, energy, atmosphere management, and resource use.

Expanded space biology: Additional consideration of microbial systems and relevant publicly available biological datasets.

Human-factors research integration: New educational activities grounded in published research on sleep, stress, communication, workload, and long-duration mission adaptation.

Optional physiological monitoring concepts: Future investigation of wearable technologies and health-related data interfaces, with appropriate privacy protections and scientific validation.

Learning and accessibility improvements: Expanded educational materials, improved device compatibility, additional languages, and further accessibility evaluation.

These are future opportunities and should not be confused with functionalities already implemented in the prototype.

14. Final Vision

Mars Survival Guide was created by Lagrange Points - Brazil around the belief that the first step toward surviving on another planet is learning to understand it.

The challenges of Mars are not limited to reaching its surface. They involve navigating an unfamiliar environment, maintaining critical resources, producing food, sustaining healthy routines, and supporting the people responsible for carrying out the mission.

Our platform approaches these challenges through three perspectives united by a common objective.

Mars Maps helps users understand where humans may explore. Mars Greenhouse helps them investigate how food-production systems might support survival. Mind Space reminds them why the human experience must remain central to mission planning.

By combining real planetary data, scientific research, mathematical methods, interactive visualization, and educational reflection, Mars Survival Guide makes complex questions about interplanetary survival more approachable.

Our intended impact is to inspire scientific curiosity, support interdisciplinary learning, and encourage a more comprehensive understanding of sustainable human exploration.

We do not present the platform as a complete solution for living on Mars. We present it as an accessible starting point for investigating the problems humanity must solve before a sustained human presence on another planet becomes possible.

Mars Survival Guide — One mission. Three perspectives. Exploring Mars means understanding its terrain, sustaining life, and caring for the people who will take us there.
